## CUDA V16 source narrative and credits
<div style="padding:27px 30px;background:#142b3b;color:#f5f8fa;border-radius:12px"><p style="color:#8fdacf;letter-spacing:2px">SQUARES IN SQUARES</p><h1 style="color:#f5f8fa">CUDA Packing Search</h1><p style="font-size:19px;color:#f5f8fa">Complementary witnesses · Spatial angle moves · CUDA gadget search</p></div>

**Certified local score: 22.366162478230. Lower is better.** Previous scored V15: **22.366246529091**.

Kirill's Union V17 keeps eight complementary Snap12 witnesses over our V15. This update preserves them, then tests signed/connected-region angle interventions and rectangular CUDA loosen-and-squeeze search followed by finer-profile recomposition. The ledger separates inherited and further-search gains.

Default **Run All** restores the frozen result on CPU and freshly certifies unchanged official metric v17 on the actual CSV and an ordinary pandas float64 round trip. Optional recomputation is disabled. Unit-square sides remain one.

## 1. Account for every increment

The score is the sum of **L(n)/sqrt(n) − 1** for n=1,…,1000. An omitted puzzle receives the official grid fallback. Per-puzzle selection keeps the shorter independently certified witness; it never averages coordinates. Counts below are sequential replacements and can overlap between stages. The ledger is a measured search trace, not an equal-budget benchmark.

[Kirill's Union V17](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-3662-cpu-cuda-mps-eda-union?scriptVersionId=361576574) preserves eight of his already-certified Snap12 witnesses when the total frontier changes. The exact imported CSV and native version are pinned. Its improvement is credited to those witnesses, not counted as our new search.

## 2. Geometry before and after

Every comparison uses the same limits in both panels. This update's changes are mostly small contact and angle changes, so their exact side reductions can be more informative than a full-layout picture. Public witness replacements are included and explicitly separated in the ledger.

## 3. Preserve complementary witnesses, then move coherent regions

A lower total score does not imply a better layout at every n. Kirill's Union V17 retains eight of his Snap12 witnesses over our V15; this update starts from that exact certified union. The earlier public construction and CUDA contributions keep their original credits.

The new finite-angle experiment changes a signed angle band or a connected spatial component instead of snapping every nearly upright square. Neighbouring squares with similar angles can move collectively while other parts of the packing stay on their previous angle branch. The same fixed-axis LP and bounded free-angle polish must repair the actual geometry. It is a finite heuristic, with controls and harmful trials retained.

## 4. Signed and connected-region angle trials

Rank layouts by the summed quarter-turn angle distance in the band **0.00002 to 0.025 radians**, divided by sqrt(n). Test a no-snap control, whole bands below 0.008/0.025, positive/negative bands, and up to three connected components with at least eight squares. Components link centres within 1.15 whose angle residues differ by less than 0.003. Duplicate masks are removed.

All arms start from the same frozen geometry and seed. A snapped start can overlap: it is not admissible until centre reclosure, free-angle refinement and independent certification succeed. Nominal budgets match within the experiment; actual iterations/time differ. No general causal or optimality claim follows from this finite search.

## 5. Squeeze reusable gadgets, then recompose on CUDA

The new rectangular CUDA run widens the eligible excess frontier from 0.80 down to 0.72 and lowers the surplus cutoff from 5 to 3, retaining leverage ranking. Its loosen/squeeze schedule explores different centres/angles and strip/L-cut seeds. This is a bounded search, not evidence that every high-leverage hypothetical improvement is attainable. Analytic gradient and square-endpoint checks accompany the run.

Two rectangular gadgets became tighter. They join the previous credited gadget bank. CUDA crop extraction and minimax staircase DP then use **64 tip bins** instead of 32, with all eight square symmetries. The finer profile can distinguish compatible joins that the coarser table conservatively discards. Final admission measures certified full-puzzle gain; a smaller gadget alone is not counted as a score improvement. Neither newly squeezed gadget appears in the final winning chains of this run. The admitted CUDA gain comes from recomposing existing certified donors; this run therefore does not demonstrate a score benefit from quenching. The largest new CUDA witness, n=923, combines crops from n=863 and the previous n=923 layout.

## 6. Readable source and optional recomputation

The compressed archive contains readable CUDA C++ and Python sources with original notices. It is decoded and hash checked, not executed during restoration. The default replay initializes no accelerator. Optional CUDA recomputation requires CuPy and compatible NVIDIA CUDA; different time budgets and hardware can change proposals. The frozen certified result remains the default whenever a proposal fails or does not improve it.

## 7. Certify the serialized file

Both checks below use the unchanged official metric v17: the exact decimal strings and an ordinary pandas float64 read/write. Rejected geometry is a failed candidate, regardless of its bounding-box estimate. All 1,000 score terms, including omitted grid fallbacks, are included.

## 1. Account for every increment

The score is the sum of **L(n)/sqrt(n) − 1** for n=1,…,1000. An omitted puzzle receives the official grid fallback. Per-puzzle selection keeps the shorter independently certified witness; it never averages coordinates. Counts below are sequential replacements and can overlap between stages. The ledger is a measured search trace, not an equal-budget benchmark.

## 2. Inspect the changed structures

The first comparison includes inherited public constructions, credited to their sources. Upright squares are grey; tilted squares are blue. Both panels for each puzzle use identical limits. A tighter portfolio can replace an entire internal structure; this is more than a change in the final decimal places.

## 3. What transfers from the new public work

| Public idea | Use in this update |
|---|---|
| Kirill's Band LP and Yang Kuang Ou's Workbench | Controlled finite angle snapping, followed by centre LP and free-angle refinement |
| Danil's Neighbour Transfer + Squeeze | Certified complementary witnesses; boundary deletion remains available in the earlier CUDA restart source |
| Alex Chilton's gadget quench and repeated fault DP | Optimize reusable pieces and compose again; its Rust `fq` was reviewed, not run here |
| Dariush Afshar's ribbon / mixed-chain construction data | Fresh donor witnesses, independently certified and explicitly credited |
| Deotte / avazaku fault composition and Janus D4 symmetries | CUDA crop/profile extraction and minimax staircase composition over all eight square symmetries |

The ribbon generator is not published in the reviewed notebook; importing those numerical witnesses is not presented as implementing that generator. A fast floating overlap screen, such as a public blend uses, does not replace the official certificate.

## 4. Finite angle moves with same-start controls

Rank layouts by the number of angles within 0.03 radians of a quarter or eighth turn, excluding angles already within 0.0003 radians. On each selected start, test thresholds **0, 0.003, 0.012, 0.03** with the same seed and nominal LP budget. Zero is the no-snap control. The centre LP must repair any overlap introduced by snapping; admissible improvements receive a bounded free-angle polish. Every final replacement still passes independent raw-decimal and pandas validation.

Harmful and failed arms are retained. This finite exploratory intervention can unlock collective motion; it does not imply that snapping every nearly aligned square is beneficial.

## 5. Recompose the updated gadgets on CUDA

A crop with footprint w×h and surplus d contains w·h+d unit squares in a box (w+f)×(h+f). Along a staircase fault, several such gadgets add their surpluses while sharing a container excess controlled by the **largest f**. Reusing a better donor can therefore improve multiple puzzles.

CUDA C++ computes crop order statistics, conservative separating-line tip profiles and the minimax DAG search. Quantized support bounds protect joins; unit-row or unit-column buffers provide alternative transitions. Reflection and transposition cover all eight symmetries. The second pass uses the newly certified construction bank. Independent full SAT screening precedes official decimal admission; the GPU's geometric estimate is not reported as a certified score.

## 6. Readable source and optional recomputation

The compressed archive contains readable CUDA C++ and Python sources with original notices. It is decoded and hash checked, not executed during restoration. The default replay initializes no accelerator. Optional CUDA recomputation requires CuPy and compatible NVIDIA CUDA; different time budgets and hardware can change proposals. The frozen certified result remains the default whenever a proposal fails or does not improve it.

## 7. Certify the serialized file

Both checks below use the unchanged official metric v17: the exact decimal strings and an ordinary pandas float64 read/write. Rejected geometry is a failed candidate, regardless of its bounding-box estimate. All 1,000 score terms, including omitted grid fallbacks, are included.

Its cpu/cuda/mps modes share the tensor operations; CPU float64 SAT, LP polishing and the unchanged official metric decide admission in every mode. This hybrid split is explicit. CUDA and MPS are configured but not hardware-tested in this release. CPU was tested locally, including independent finite-difference gradient checks and a real recomputation/official-admission test. No GPU or MPS was used for our local result.

The default run restores pinned inputs and fixed-point new witnesses, then freshly certifies raw decimals and a default pandas float64 round trip. RUN_SEARCH enables optional recomputation on the selected backend. MPS requires a local Mac and is unavailable on Kaggle. Square side lengths stay one; only centres move for numerical clearance. No optimality or algorithm-invention claim is made.

# Public notebook narrative and source attribution

## 1. Where the gain comes from

For each n, keep the smallest independently certified container. The metric is the sum of **L / sqrt(n) − 1** over n = 1,…,1000. Omitted puzzles receive the official grid score.

The new public union retains 13 complementary witnesses from Sung Heo's pinned dashboard and 45 from Dariush Afshar's newer construction output. Kirill's Edge LP output adds no further wins after that union. Dariush's 45 rows are labelled `construction` in his source table; their gain belongs to his search. Earlier mathematical construction and witness credits remain attached.

The next stages are independent implementations tested here. Counts are accepted stage replacements and may include the same n twice. Stage gains are sequential accounting, not a causal ablation.

## 5. Readable source and optional recomputation

The following archive restores the exact readable Python and CUDA C++ source, credited geometry helpers and unchanged official metric. SHA256 guards the archive and all frozen inputs. Default execution needs NumPy, pandas, SciPy, matplotlib and a compatible mpmath. The optional CUDA branch also needs CuPy, PyTorch and an NVIDIA driver with NVRTC; the Kaggle GPU image supplies this stack. CPU replay does not import CUDA libraries.

Enable `RECOMPUTE_LP` for a bounded 24-layout dual-guided pass or `RECOMPUTE_CUDA` for the 32-bin CUDA composition. Each starts from the frozen best, and admission is monotone. GPU memory is checked before allocating the profile table; this configuration needs approximately 6 GB free device memory. Results may vary with finite solver budgets and numerical libraries. The frozen default CSV is byte-exact.

# Current pinned Capacity Union V1

# Upstream sources

The final-two-submission continuation on 7 November 2026 refreshed Kirill Tymchishin's [Contact LP](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-2234-cpu-cuda-mps-eda-contact-lp), exact CSV `3bf2c2bdd6e4df14e73e6c2688d4501d3e90467be82b93ab112ffe83b0752b76`, and Living Atlas's later output, exact CSV `986933600b2ed3c6a10a0015b540ce80f3bdc5e3881c6924015c2fe5d699d5c7`. The public n803 packing improves the enclosing side to28.821397014543354, with small public n595/n970 refinements. This project's subsequent nonlinear restoration lowers n595 to24.863748345836544 and n970 to31.639109896136. All geometry passes the unchanged official metric after the ordinary pandas round trip. Snapshot hashes, sources, notices and per-puzzle import receipts are preserved under `research/final_two_20261107/`.

`sis/gpu_rectangle_search.py` generates an inspected variable-rectangle CUDA variant of lightningv08's Apache-2.0 L-BFGS skeleton. The rectangular objective, common-overhang derivative, soft-to-unit continuation, denser/sparser piece surgery, independent CPU-gradient controls and cross-puzzle admission are implemented in this project. The completed Kaggle run tested3,456 trajectories and produced zero additional geometric gain. `sis/gpu_stack_search.py` tested1,152 full-stack trajectories and also produced zero additional gain. These failed searches must not be credited with the newer public baseline or the independently found CPU refinements. Their exact saved-version outputs, hardware checks, logs and certificates are preserved under `artifacts/final_two_gpu_rectangle_v2/` and `artifacts/final_two_gpu_stack_v1/`.

`sis/cross_surgery.py` is this project's exact polygon-area strip selection, informed by Evan Daniel's MIT L-cut experiments; thirty native refinements yielded zero gain. `sis/rectangular_window_search.py` extends this project's exact sweep-line window search to all origins of rectangles. The2,169 historical donor layouts preserve their original source hashes and notices;225,560 crop tests found nine improved donor crops, whose recomposition yielded no whole-puzzle gain. `sis/contact_milp.py` jointly selects fixed-angle separating faces with Big-M values derived from explicit coordinate bounds. After inspected solver-interface repairs, eight bounded trials gave zero gain; time limits are not geometric optimality proofs. Failed interface runs and the invalid native rectangular control remain saved separately and were never admitted. All62 current tests pass.

The later 7 November continuation retains [Kirill Tymchishin's Union LP](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-2235-cpu-cuda-mps-eda-union-lp), public run12:06:38 UTC, exact CSV SHA-256 `178c4ca3f40b33d0994259e433709ce4952ebf8b3dfd5120a51c4144a145016a`. It contributes a tiny independently admitted n991 refinement. Its original Apache-2.0, Levy-source license and source notices are preserved in `vendor/union_lp/` and in the downloaded snapshot. The incomplete public CSV has553 explicit puzzles; this project's complete portfolio retains its existing certified geometries for every other size.

The fresh donor recomposition improves n597,647,753,809 using existing n416,n417,n699,n753 layouts. The source n699 is the newer Samanyu public improvement. The accepted chains use no newly generated pose or column-phase donor. A matched21-bin run using exactly the same donors attains the same minimum fractions; the gain therefore belongs to fresh donor recomposition, not to an established advantage of continuous clearances. Full recipes and the matched experiment are preserved under runs/exact_fresh_public18/ and runs/matched_quantized_public18/. Additional fixed-container contact restoration lowers n753 further.

`sis/native/exact_dp.cpp` is this project's sparse continuous-clearance skyline DP. `sis/exact_composition.py` generates an inspected exact-Pareto variant of the Apache-2.0 Boxed In extractor and retains original/generated source hashes. Exactness refers to the supplied finite profiles and staircase transition rules; interval certification independently judges the actual geometry. `sis/column_phase_search.py` implements independent slides of tilted tiling columns, informed by the Erdos--Graham lattice described by lostdecimal27. Its24-trial pilot reached none of the target cardinalities and its16 retained positive-surplus layouts yielded no further whole-puzzle gain. All inputs and losing checkpoints are preserved.

The 7 November 2026 12:00 UTC follow-up retrieved [samanyu1808's sis-submit](https://www.kaggle.com/code/samanyu1808/sis-submit), latest public run timestamp 11:36:37 UTC. Its exact CSV SHA-256 is `ec737eb4357c72bdf4c1f1c902c5dc5eb3c7a8c000220a9fad508f3fce841bb9`. Twenty better individual packings pass the unchanged current official metric when combined with portfolio16, giving certified local portfolio17 score **22.223436812666854**. The total additional gain **0.000367176480** belongs to the public source and its credited packing authors, Evan Daniel MIT optimizer, and stretch/quench contributors. Exact notebook source, output, per-file hashes and the combined certificate are retained under `research/below20_20261107/public_1200/samanyu/`.

`sis/island_search.py` implements this project's coherent band/block model, rigid-body transforms, aggregated force/torque gradient, large coordinated mutations, and release to individual unit-square restoration. Every input body is retained in the partition; each macro rotation applies to both centers and square orientations. Independent tests check exact internal separation and the chain rule, including box-wall derivatives and temporary body sizes. This search is an experimental construction change; the public-source baseline gains above are not attributed to this model.

Retrieved on 6 November 2026. Public packings retain the original authors' credits.

* `official_metric.py`: [Kaggle's current official metric](https://www.kaggle.com/code/metric/squares-in-squares), downloaded through `kaggle kernels pull`. SHA-256: `dc850dadb8c3e7b36ddc2ddf27f514e88c3b0c62662dd4bd1e1bc450b5604b44`. This file is unmodified. The current metric has tighter coordinate/angle/literal bounds and padded AABB sweeping compared with the copy embedded in Atlas v82.
* `atlas/cuda_backend.py`, `atlas/cuda_precision.py`, `atlas/contact_polish.py`, `atlas/search_geometry.py`: unmodified files from the [Living Atlas v82 output](https://www.kaggle.com/code/malyshevdanil/squares-in-squares-living-atlas-of-tight-packings), whose comments attribute the CUDA L-BFGS, conservative SAT, and contact LP implementation to [lightningv08](https://www.kaggle.com/code/lightningv08/squares-in-squares-cuda-packing-search), Apache 2.0, with background credit to prvsiyan.
* Initial packing bank: Atlas v82 `submission.csv`, SHA-256 `a0fbe90b61234490917b023510c9507213b274db97bf47caad767170240cd55a`. The Atlas notebook's full source, source table, validation report, and all downloaded output files are retained locally under `research/reference/`. Its public source citations include Francisco Couzo, Evan Daniel, Joshua Levy, Erich Friedman, the original construction authors, and the public Kaggle notebook contributors listed in the Atlas notebook.

The files in `sis/` implement this project's orchestration, independent SAT geometry, fixed-angle compaction, search scheduling, and submission handling. Public packing coordinates are derived data and retain all upstream attribution. A floating candidate is accepted only after the unchanged current official metric certifies the serialized pandas round trip.

The observed targets in `research/frontier_targets.csv` come from [inversion's public per-puzzle leaderboard, version 25](https://www.kaggle.com/code/inversion/squares-in-squares-per-puzzle-leaderboard). They are search targets, not known coordinates or proofs of optimality.

The latest [Francisco Couzo certificate manifest](https://github.com/franciscouzo/square-packing/tree/712c6a6e9ef58a9521784e6b7e236af813422de7) was checked at commit `712c6a6e9ef58a9521784e6b7e236af813422de7` (28 October 2026). No manifest bound improved the Atlas bank directly.

Additional research inputs retrieved on 6 November 2026:

* [Evan Daniel and contributors](https://github.com/evand/square-packing/tree/bb4cc78e5b35103c1f177db55e9cf08974e66563), pinned commit `bb4cc78e5b35103c1f177db55e9cf08974e66563`, MIT. All 461 certificates were audited; seven gave direct improvements, and their geometries also supplied staircase compositions. Original notices are preserved in the archive.
* [kmmmvs' Squares Public Merge Daily](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kmmmvs/squares-public-merge-daily), including the source's credited public contributors. The imported coordinates improved n=933 and n=995 materially and several other sizes slightly. The exact imported file and receipt are under `research/daily_merge/` and `runs/daily_merge_import/`.
* [prvsiyan's A Square Deal | Research to Verified Packings](https://www.kaggle.com/code/prvsiyan/a-square-deal-research-to-verified-packings), the public run dated 6 November 2026, 15:13 UTC. Its output CSV SHA-256 is `4af701e9512ae1baf2e751429d05e74a245f00f1abc2bbe81f7e5df8f2231a76`. Twenty-five small coordinate refinements were imported; after independent certification their total additional gain is approximately 0.0000013046. This is a public-source refinement, not a demonstrated gain from this project's neural model. Its notebook, metadata, output, and log are retained under `research/prvsiyan/latest/`.

The portable neural proposal model is this project's 1,505-parameter MLP, fitted on 1,792 actual optimizer outcomes with entire puzzle sizes held out. SHA-256: `7028a3172b7564d426bf14009b35211e078ba9d1b8c707b17f10d008fc903504`. Lower residual penalties have been demonstrated; a leaderboard gain from the model has not. CPU geometry and square-window cropping in `sis/cpu_backend.py` and `sis/window_search.py` are implemented in this project and checked against independent geometric calculations.

The structural arm-transfer method in `sis/arm_transfers.py` is implemented in this project, inspired by [3정훈's Stretching good packings to nearby n](https://www.kaggle.com/code/az05192000gmailcom/22-2401-stretching-good-packings-to-nearby-n). Its public notebook was retrieved under `research/strip_transfer/`. The method copies or removes complete tilted-arm stacks and upright rows/columns, then uses this project's float64 CPU optimizer. Orientation grouping, multiple cuts and seed screening are implemented here; no external binary is executed. The first pilot generated 5,821 proposals, refined 80 selected sizes and produced officially certified improvements at n=685, 689 and 936, with a combined gain of 0.000271819264. # Completed multiple-square capacity search v1

Source: https://www.kaggle.com/code/penguin069/squares-multiple-insertion-capacity-search (saved version 1).

The completed two-T4 notebook explores twelve rectangular counts with 2, 4 or 6 added whole squares. The saved output independently certifies at 22.216243812500682, improving n498, n591 and n641 by a total 0.0010173904293466762 against its bound baseline. All 1,000 puzzles and 500,500 rows pass the current official metric after its default pandas round trip.

The strongest saved-input union additionally retains the earlier Module Capacity control refinements and Kirill Tymchishin's saved Two-size LP v16 n998 refinement. Its independent forecast is 22.216243763098966. A leaderboard score below 20 remains unachieved.

The archive preserves all original input hashes, source cells and 558 checkpoint files. It contains 144 exported donors and 12,528 GPU trajectories. The matched audit checks 5,104 starting-profile pairs and 673 native comparisons. Shared descendant populations prevent an independent causal interpretation of later comparisons; the local and equal-area uniform arms have roughly balanced wins. The gain is certified from complete hard unit-square layouts after recomposition.

The additional 2,487-donor / 1,121,039-profile local scan completed 4,341,866,653 transitions without further improvement. Conditional forecasts and rounded intermediate states are excluded from this union.

Original public coordinate, geometry, optimizer and source-specific notices are retained in the bound source bundle. The newer public input attribution is preserved in vendor/public_notices/public_refresh_20261108_1800/SOURCE_NOTICES.md and its verbatim upstream notices. This result does not transfer the original contributors' discovery credit or licenses.

# Squares in Squares Evolutionary Contact Search

Starting local certified score: **22.221247700720**. The notebook carries all 1,000 puzzles and 500,500 true unit squares. Each size is independent; smaller total `sum(L_n/sqrt(n)-1)` is better.

The November 8 refresh imports 60 improved public layouts from Kirill Tymchishin's EDA+n632 LP, Living Atlas, Nilanjan Saha and Daily Merge. Their additional 0.001629651804 gain is attributed to the public sources and their upstream authors. Our stronger existing n446, n595, n803 and n918 packings survive the merge.

The first local GA/covariance/contact campaign tested 740 proposals and accepted 20 records. It improved the public portfolio24 by 0.000126353560 before the newer public refresh. A further 216-trial evolutionary campaign on the new baseline improves n371, n595 and n632 by 0.000006389967. The new n632 record comes from native contact polishing. A paired scaled LP campaign tested 72 trials and found smaller n632 gains that do not beat that native record. These contributions are kept distinct from imported public gains.

The prior TPU-host notebook completed 15,046 distinct refinements over 200 sizes using 96 workers on 224 usable vCPUs and 377.836 GiB RAM. All four improvements against its old baseline came from its random control; learned ranking produced zero. Those four packings are already superseded. This version carries the stronger baseline and searches feasible box side with inherited structural mutations and covariance-guided rigid band moves.

A score below 20 remains unachieved. All starting and final records use true unit squares and the unchanged current metric after ordinary pandas serialization. Source-specific notices, software licenses, exact checkpoints and hashes are retained.

The completed reusable-module follow-up tested 540 native trials across nine binding rectangular modules. It reduced the 148-square module used by n632/n684 and the 173-square n595 module. Exact continuous-clearance recomposition independently certifies the resulting whole-puzzle improvements. The final source record includes 391,584 extracted profiles and the full mutated/restored endpoints. The latest complete local portfolio34 certifies at 22.221280677171318, compared with the confirmed version1 score 22.2213143183. The module overhang fitness is never itself counted as a competition score.

A subsequent 320-trial module run adds larger lattice-column glides and seam slips along the tilted edge direction. The n446 module improves from0.6300432333989399 to0.6294400867126644: a four-square column glides by-0.2, a five-square seam slips by+0.2, and native contact restoration refines descendants. Recomposition across392738 profiles confirms a genuine n446 whole-packing improvement. The exported geometry remains true unit squares and passes current official certification. The new local portfolio36 also retains the latest public n597 packing. This version distinguishes the public n597 gain from the original n446 glide gain.


Independent searches inherit locally optimized descendants and retain every proposal and official record. The population search combines aligned whole-pose crossover, elite retention and structural mutations. The covariance search learns correlated translations and rotations of whole tilted regions. Every record is checked with the unchanged current official metric after the default pandas round trip. The final merge admits only valid improvements over this complete starting file.

The chosen accelerator supplies host CPUs. Geometric optimization runs in float64 on CPU, using the pinned MIT fq executable and independent LP/SAT/interval gates. Actual CPU affinity, cgroup quota and RAM determine concurrency. The local model comparison produced no model gains; no learned-policy gain is assumed here.

Our new experiment follows a full bounded randomized separation-graph scan with paired free-angle contact LP arms. Actual wall times and iterations can differ, so this is a finite descriptive paired experiment rather than a universal causal or speed claim. Independent full geometry, quantized decimals and the unchanged official metric decide admission. We never assume a positive effect of regularization before seeing the paired results.

No metric tolerances are changed and no mathematical-record claim is made.

## 2. Geometry before and after

Every comparison uses the same limits in both panels. This update's changes are mostly small contact and angle changes, so their exact side reductions can be more informative than a full-layout picture. Public witness replacements are included and explicitly separated in the ledger.

## 3. Preserve complementary witnesses, then move coherent regions

A lower total score does not imply a better layout at every n. Kirill's Union V17 retains eight of his Snap12 witnesses over our V15; this update starts from that exact certified union. The earlier public construction and CUDA contributions keep their original credits.

The new finite-angle experiment changes a signed angle band or a connected spatial component instead of snapping every nearly upright square. Neighbouring squares with similar angles can move collectively while other parts of the packing stay on their previous angle branch. The same fixed-axis LP and bounded free-angle polish must repair the actual geometry. It is a finite heuristic, with controls and harmful trials retained.

## 4. Signed and connected-region angle trials

Rank layouts by the summed quarter-turn angle distance in the band **0.00002 to 0.025 radians**, divided by sqrt(n). Test a no-snap control, whole bands below 0.008/0.025, positive/negative bands, and up to three connected components with at least eight squares. Components link centres within 1.15 whose angle residues differ by less than 0.003. Duplicate masks are removed.

All arms start from the same frozen geometry and seed. A snapped start can overlap: it is not admissible until centre reclosure, free-angle refinement and independent certification succeed. Nominal budgets match within the experiment; actual iterations/time differ. No general causal or optimality claim follows from this finite search.

## 5. Squeeze reusable gadgets, then recompose on CUDA

The new rectangular CUDA run widens the eligible excess frontier from 0.80 down to 0.72 and lowers the surplus cutoff from 5 to 3, retaining leverage ranking. Its loosen/squeeze schedule explores different centres/angles and strip/L-cut seeds. This is a bounded search, not evidence that every high-leverage hypothetical improvement is attainable. Analytic gradient and square-endpoint checks accompany the run.

Two rectangular gadgets became tighter. They join the previous credited gadget bank. CUDA crop extraction and minimax staircase DP then use **64 tip bins** instead of 32, with all eight square symmetries. The finer profile can distinguish compatible joins that the coarser table conservatively discards. Final admission measures certified full-puzzle gain; a smaller gadget alone is not counted as a score improvement. Neither newly squeezed gadget appears in the final winning chains of this run. The admitted CUDA gain comes from recomposing existing certified donors; this run therefore does not demonstrate a score benefit from quenching. The largest new CUDA witness, n=923, combines crops from n=863 and the previous n=923 layout.

## 4. Finite angle moves with same-start controls

Rank layouts by the number of angles within 0.03 radians of a quarter or eighth turn, excluding angles already within 0.0003 radians. ## 5. Recompose the updated gadgets on CUDA

A crop with footprint w×h and surplus d contains w·h+d unit squares in a box (w+f)×(h+f). Along a staircase fault, several such gadgets add their surpluses while sharing a container excess controlled by the **largest f**. Reusing a better donor can therefore improve multiple puzzles.

CUDA C++ computes crop order statistics, conservative separating-line tip profiles and the minimax DAG search. Quantized support bounds protect joins; unit-row or unit-column buffers provide alternative transitions. Reflection and transposition cover all eight symmetries. The second pass uses the newly certified construction bank. Independent full SAT screening precedes official decimal admission; the GPU's geometric estimate is not reported as a certified score.

# Public notebook narrative and source attribution

## 1. Where the gain comes from

For each n, keep the smallest independently certified container. The metric is the sum of **L / sqrt(n) − 1** over n = 1,…,1000. Omitted puzzles receive the official grid score.

The new public union retains 13 complementary witnesses from Sung Heo's pinned dashboard and 45 from Dariush Afshar's newer construction output. Kirill's Edge LP output adds no further wins after that union. Dariush's 45 rows are labelled `construction` in his source table; their gain belongs to his search. Earlier mathematical construction and witness credits remain attached.

The next stages are independent implementations tested here. Counts are accepted stage replacements and may include the same n twice. Stage gains are sequential accounting, not a causal ablation.

## 5. Readable source and optional recomputation

The following archive restores the exact readable Python and CUDA C++ source, credited geometry helpers and unchanged official metric. SHA256 guards the archive and all frozen inputs. Default execution needs NumPy, pandas, SciPy, matplotlib and a compatible mpmath. The optional CUDA branch also needs CuPy, PyTorch and an NVIDIA driver with NVRTC; the Kaggle GPU image supplies this stack. CPU replay does not import CUDA libraries.

Enable `RECOMPUTE_LP` for a bounded 24-layout dual-guided pass or `RECOMPUTE_CUDA` for the 32-bin CUDA composition. Each starts from the frozen best, and admission is monotone. GPU memory is checked before allocating the profile table; this configuration needs approximately 6 GB free device memory. Results may vary with finite solver budgets and numerical libraries. The frozen default CSV is byte-exact.

# Squares in Squares - Living Atlas of Tight Packings

Start from the attached **Fresh Records, Certified** notebook output, then merge the newest public packings puzzle by puzzle and replay this notebook's own certified improvements.

**Version 110 (09 November):** the attached public outputs complement each other, and the best single one (kirilltym's 22 2158 cpu cuda mps eda n591 trust lp, 22.2157958) is not the best packing for every `n`.
The merge also considers 0 stored packings (`n` = ) carried forward from earlier versions: local CUDA L-BFGS search, CPU contact-LP polishing, and external packings credited below. Each is retained only where it is the smallest certified packing. The combined result is **22.2157956483**, compared with 22.2157958348 for the best single attached notebook.

Each public packing is admitted only after the same float64 round trip and official certification; border expansion and deletion then run on the merged packings.
Coordinates are round-trip doubles, and centre dilation opens contacts by about `1e-11`. The final CSV is read with pandas' default float64 parser and scored exactly as on Kaggle.
Earlier versions replayed 60 GPU-search gains from 22 October; public packings have since beaten all of them, so their data was replaced by the version 7 improvements.

The default run replays compressed, locally found coordinates. The full search implementation is included below; `RECOMPUTE_SEARCH=True` reruns a bounded search and can take substantially longer.

## Official metric and certification library

Both are embedded verbatim from the certified base. All admission checks use the unchanged competition metric.

## Load the attached base

The parent notebook is the only packing input. Its own credits and source provenance remain applicable.

## Reproducible search code

The extracted CUDA L-BFGS, SAT continuation and contact LP are adapted from lightningv08 (Apache-2.0). Seed selection, checkpointing and the local search schedule are provided here. Floating search candidates still require certification.

## Replay, certify, and write

Every candidate is checked on the exact decimal strings that will be written. The complete 1000-puzzle output is certified again.

## Merge with the newest public packings

Public notebooks move fast. Each attached public output is compared puzzle by puzzle with the packing above.
A smaller public packing replaces ours only if it passes the official metric after the same float64 round trip the scorer uses.
If the best one fails, the next best is tried.

## Score the final float64 file

Default `pd.read_csv` followed by the official `score()` reproduces the leaderboard read path.

Before this refresh, every puzzle in our V16 output

## What the task measures and what the research suggests

For every n=1…1000, place n unit squares with centres (x,y) and angles θ.
They may rotate but their interiors must not overlap. Minimize
`sum(L_n / sqrt(n) - 1)`, where L_n is the enclosing square side. The area
bound is sqrt(n); the simple grid gives ceil(sqrt(n)).

* [Arslanov, Mustafin and Shangitbayev (2021)](https://doi.org/10.37236/8586)
  give constructions beating the grid for n=m²−m, m≥12. This shows why tilted,
  structured layouts matter; it is not a recipe for a global optimum.
* [The Squares Project methods survey](https://squaremath.org/papers/square-packing-methods-survey.html)
  explains separating-axis cells, fixed-angle LP, rotational SLP, and certification.
  With angles and one separating branch per pair fixed, centres and container
  size enter linear inequalities. Moving angles requires linearization and a
  subsequent nonlinear feasibility check.
* [Ostashev's first-party research account](https://ostashev.ai/square-packing/)
  combines structured seeds with local polishing and exact checks. We preserve
  existing layouts rather than starting large instances from randomness.
* [Addis, Locatelli and Schoen: Disk Packing in a Square](https://optimization-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2005/10/1229.pdf)
  motivates perturb-then-refine basin proposals. That paper concerns disks;
  our square version uses separating-axis overlap penalties and is an adaptation.

The added method is a local heuristic, not a new mathematical construction or
proof. Numerical gains must survive the competition's interval checker.

   its serialized coordinates and the per-puzzle score improves.
4. Preserve every unmodified decimal coordinate string; export an audit trail.

The additional refinement is small. It is a local heuristic, with no claim of
global optimality, a new mathematical construction, or a substantial new record.

## Two independent whole-group changes

Each complete n contributes L / √n − 1, with L the enclosing side. The all-size screen found a material n684 replacement common to Fault-line V55, Starter V58 and the Atlas V110 intermediate file. We use the fixed Fault-line V55 numerical source with its public credits.

For projection p and the sum h of the two square supports on a separating axis, dilating centres by α changes the separating margin from |p| − h to α|p| − h. The affine recipe raises the minimum SAT margin toward 2 × 10⁻¹¹ while leaving every square side and angle intact. The unchanged official verifier checks the serialized whole group.

For n591 the existing contact model linearizes a separating axis for each nearby pair and the enclosing box. Write displacements as r z and constrain the centre variables to |z| ≤ 1. Compare radii 4 × 10⁻⁷ and 1.2 × 10⁻⁶, with fixed angles or an angular bound of 0.4r. Each arm has a 512-round cap and a 20-second budget tested between rounds. Exact geometry admits each accepted nonlinear step.

## Unchanged metric and visible search implementation

The official V20 source is hash-checked without changing its geometry rules. Our CPU contact LP linearizes active separating axes inside a small trust region; fixed-angle and free-angle controls use the same export clearance. The original portable CPU/CUDA/MPS routes remain available. This version runs CPU only. The earlier T4 smoke is historical, and MPS has not been tested on hardware.

The donor group is read from fixed V55. Its affine recipe is displayed below and verified against the exact expected serialized coordinate strings. The only compacted data are the new own n591 coordinates. The exporter replaces those two complete layouts and streams the remaining rows directly from V25.

The selected n591 arm used free angles, accepted 82 steps and ran locally for 8.490 seconds. The four arms are alternatives from the same V25 start. The comparison treats n684 as a separate inherited contribution and displays the physical effect of the guard.

# Contact LP + Cusp Bounds

Two new complete unit-square packings, **N=465 and N=998**, improve the frozen public top-1 available on 8 November 2026. The numerical bank is inherited; the two changed packings are our search contribution.

| Comparison | Official score, lower is better |
|---|---:|
| Penguin069 Capacity Discoveries Certified Union, V1 | 22.216243763099026 |
| This frozen candidate, expected | 22.216233022107896 |
| Own gain on the two changed N | **0.00001074099113** |

This is a local refinement, not a new global packing bound. Default execution reconstructs the exact CSV and runs fresh official raw-decimal and ordinary-pandas validation on **all 1000 N**. The final cells offer a separate bounded search replay. No GPU, downloaded executable bundle, hidden numerical payload or silent baseline refresh is used.

## Frozen inputs

Attach these two inputs: [Capacity Discoveries Certified Union, saved V1](https://www.kaggle.com/code/penguin069/squares-capacity-discoveries-certified-union?scriptVersionId=367038751), and [our two numerical witnesses](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/avazaku/squares-contact-lp-cusp-bounds-465-998).

The first input supplies the inherited bank. The second supplies 1463 transparent CSV rows, the unmodified official metric, source notices and study receipts. Input hashes below are mandatory. We never execute source code from an upstream notebook or dataset.

## Why change the LP near cardinal contacts?

A standard contact LP linearizes the selected separating projection and square support. At a relative angle near a multiple of 90 degrees, the support contains an absolute-value cusp. A derivative at the current angle may miss the other side of the cusp inside the trust interval.

We use Kirill Tymchishin's scaled displacement variables, $\Delta=r z$, with $|z_x|,|z_y|\le1$ and $|z_\theta|\le0.4$. Let $\xi$ be the relative angle wrapped to $[-\pi/4,\pi/4)$ and $d$ its change. Near a cusp:

$$\frac{1+|\cos(\xi+d)|+|\sin(\xi+d)|}{2}
\le \frac{1+\cos\xi-\sin\xi\,d+|\xi+d|}{2}.$$

Two linear inequalities, one for each sign, represent the absolute-value bound. We apply the analogous bound to square-wall support. The radius is restricted to $0<r\le0.01$, so the local concavity range used by the bound is valid. **Only support is majorized**; the rotating separating projection is still linearized. Therefore every step is backtracked, retracted with a small centre dilation, checked against true SAT, and admitted by the official interval metric before export.

The LP proposal obeys trust bounds. Centre-dilation retraction can move the accepted centres beyond those proposal boxes; it does not resize the unit squares. The pair radius includes all potentially colliding pairs. The final CSV is never made from fractional, rounded-square or soft-overlap states.

## Independent C++ geometry check

HiGHS solves the sparse LP through SciPy. The following small C++17 hard-SAT kernel provides an independent FP64 energy/gradient implementation. It is compiled without fast-math and checked against NumPy. It is not a replacement for the official interval evaluator.

## Whole-portfolio validation

Each representation starts in a fresh process, checks every explicit N, and uses no cached verdicts or grid fallback. Ordinary pandas inference is deliberate: decimal strings that pass one representation can fail another. The adversarial precision check below demonstrates this difference.

## Controlled observations and limits

The search was developed on the earlier Penguin Kernel Union V1. A later public top-1 appeared during validation. We retained only our two independently generated witnesses and rechecked them against the new Capacity Union V1. Its structural capacity discoveries and all other inherited improvements belong to their original authors.

The table below reports the original matched studies. At N=998 both continuation arms share the same first accepted cusp step; the adaptive-policy arms then share the same accepted continuation endpoint. At N=465 both arms share its first accepted cusp step. Common-start gains are not counted again as an arm's incremental gain.

Budgets are ceilings, not equal-work experiments. Actual times differ, early stops differ, and trajectories are not independent statistical samples. `seconds` in a search trace measures the LP call; the outer time ceiling is checked between iterations. No equal-FLOP or broad solver-speed claim is made.

The saved pilot solved four identical models with dual-simplex and interior-point methods. On N=998 the cusp model reached a valid decreasing endpoint with `highs-ipm`; its dual-simplex run reached the 8-second limit. This is one observed model, not a universal speed result. N=543 produced no admitted improvement. N=970 ended in a solver numerical error and is not evidence of no possible gain. The bounded refinement covers two winning N; it does not establish their optimality.

## Optional standalone search replay

Default execution above uses the frozen accepted witnesses, so validation does not depend on optimizer timing. To rerun the controlled search, attach the original [Penguin Kernel Union saved V1](https://www.kaggle.com/code/penguin069/squares-kernel-union-certified-portfolio?scriptVersionId=366974465) input and set `RUN_SEARCH=True`. This is a separate bounded experiment. LP paths and coordinates depend on solver version, platform and elapsed-time cutoffs; bitwise numerical replay is not promised.

The script exports only whole packings passing both official raw and ordinary-pandas checks and improving their pinned study warm start. Search files go into `optional_replay/`, never silently replace the already validated root `submission.csv`. To submit another result, recompose and run the full gates again.

New code and adaptations are released under Apache-2.0 subject to retained upstream notices. Numerical packing attribution and code licensing are separate: this notebook does not grant a blanket relicense of upstream coordinate records. The accompanying dataset preserves those notices and contains ordinary readable CSV, JSON and Python files.

## Preserved Avazaku16 original Markdown

# Contact LP + Cusp Bounds

Five new whole packings improve the **frozen Kirill Complement LP V18** bank. Its public geometry and earlier capacity discoveries are inherited. Our contribution is the measured refinement at **N=465, 498, 591, 641 and 998**.

| Comparison | Total score, lower is better |
|---|---:|
| Frozen public V18 baseline | 22.21623264163536 |
| This candidate, expected before this Run All validates it | 22.216214050705222 |
| Own reduction over that bank | **0.00001859093014** |
| Our cusp/IPM uniform-retraction control: reduction | 0.00001356289408 |
| Additional correction-portfolio advantage | **0.00000502803605** |

Default execution reconstructs the exact frozen CSV and freshly validates all 1000 explicit N through raw-decimal and ordinary-pandas paths. Optional matched search is separate and off. Five full geometries change, including individual angles and relative centres, not only translation or scalar dilation. No numerical payload is hidden in code.

## Frozen inputs

Attach [Kirill Tymchishin's Complement LP, saved V18](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-2162-cpu-cuda-mps-eda-complement-lp?scriptVersionId=367069341) and version4 of [our existing witness dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/avazaku/squares-contact-lp-cusp-bounds-465-998).

The source has 553 explicit public groups. Its 447 missing default grids are materialized exactly, with zero claimed search gain. The dataset supplies 3193 readable witness rows, measured controls and preserved notices. We read upstream numerical CSVs only. The official evaluator is copied unchanged after its SHA check.

## Cusp-aware main LP

The coupled LP retains Prvsiyan/lightningv08 geometry and Kirill's scaled variables $\Delta=r z$, with $|z_x|,|z_y|\le1$ and $|z_\theta|\le0.4$. Every centre and angle is a main-model variable. Wrap the relative angle to $\xi\in[-\pi/4,\pi/4)$ and let $d$ be its change. Near a cardinal cusp:

$$\frac{1+|\cos(\xi+d)|+|\sin(\xi+d)|}{2}
\le\frac{1+\cos\xi-\sin\xi\,d+|\xi+d|}{2}.$$

Two affine inequalities implement the absolute value; wall support uses the analogous bound. Radius $0<r\le0.01$ stays in the local concavity range. Only support is majorized: the rotating separating projection is still linearized. LP feasibility alone is not a physical certificate.

## A second LP for the full nonlinear trial

Both arms solve the same cusp/IPM main LP and try 19 uniform-retraction backtracks. The experimental arm also fixes the full trial's angles and optimizes every centre and the container side. For each selected signed separating axis $a_{ij}$:

$$a_{ij}\cdot(v_i-v_j)\le a_{ij}\cdot(c_j-c_i)-R_{ij}-\varepsilon.$$

With fixed angles and axes these inequalities are exact. Radius $\sqrt2+2\sqrt2\eta+10^{-4}$ includes every potentially colliding pair under bounded correction motion. We use $\eta=\max(r,10^{-4})$ and retain the better endpoint: correction or ordinary retraction.

This permits O(r) additional centre movement, not merely O(r²) residual repair. We measure the added LP as a whole. Dilation can move accepted centres beyond proposal boxes; unit-square dimensions remain unchanged. Selected branches restrict the local model. Accepted states get hard SAT checks; exported endpoints require official raw and ordinary-pandas admission. No global optimality follows.

## Independent geometry and precision checks

The C++17 hard-SAT kernel is a separate FP64 implementation, checked against NumPy and compiled without fast-math. It does not replace official interval arithmetic. Small tests cover valid grids/rotations, overlap, coordinate bounds, an overlap hidden by float64 rounding, and fixed-angle polygon/support references.

## Controlled observations and limits

The control is our cusp/IPM solver with uniform retraction, not an exact reproduction of Kirill's algorithm. Both arms have the same pinned start, main model, tolerances, trust policy and ceilings. Correction adds LP work; later states and models can diverge.

N465/998 used 160-round, 100-second ceilings. N498/591/641 used 60-round, 35-second ceilings; those targets were chosen from newly inherited capacity constructions before their new solves. Ceilings are soft: construction, retraction and admission add time. Actual runtimes and counts differ. These finite observations do not establish equal-work or general superiority.

**Historical audit scope:** 676 accepted main solutions and 686 saved states received independent checks, including all-pairs C++ SAT. All 10 final control/experimental endpoints passed raw and pandas, and unchanged CSV groups/source hashes were checked. However, 35 successful but rejected main proposals did not retain their solutions. Their residual audit is incomplete: overall `passed=False`, separately `candidate_gates_passed=True`. Those unused proposals are not in the output. We do not claim every proposal residual was audited. The full-file gates below independently validate the submitted portfolio.

## Fresh full-file admission

Each representation starts fresh validator processes and checks all 1000 explicit groups with no geometry cache. Rejection fails the run; no invalid group is silently replaced by a grid. Both totals must agree and match the frozen expected score. The 447 default grids were materialized before validation, not inserted as fallbacks after failures.

## Optional matched replay

`RUN_SEARCH=False` keeps default output independent of optimizer timing. Set it to True to replay both arms from the same Kirill input using original per-N ceilings. Solver version, platform, instrumentation and time cutoffs can change trajectories; bitwise optimization replay is not promised.

Files stay in `optional_replay/`, never replacing root `submission.csv`. Both official parsers must accept an endpoint before export. Changed results require recomposition and full gates before submission. The CLI accepts smaller `--rounds`/`--seconds` limits for functional checks, not as reproductions of reported study results.

## Sources and reuse

- Frozen bank and scaled LP variables: [Kirill Tymchishin, Complement LP V18](https://www.kaggle.com/code/kirilltym/22-2162-cpu-cuda-mps-eda-complement-lp?scriptVersionId=367069341). Its Penguin capacity geometry and earlier public improvements remain inherited.
- Coupled contact LP and kink-aware geometry: Prvsiyan/lightningv08, with retained Apache-2.0 attribution. Our earlier cusp treatment and accepted-step policy remain visible in `search.py`; this update measures the additional fixed-angle correction LP.
- Numerical lineage includes Penguin069, Malyshev Danil, Nilanjan Saha, Busyaprime, Alex Chilton after Chris Deotte, Francisco Couzo, Evan Daniel, Joshua Levy and contributors named in the preserved `release_artifacts/UPSTREAM_SOURCE_NOTICES.md`. Existing source-specific notices and coordinate conditions remain intact.
- Optimization uses [SciPy/HiGHS](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/optimize.linprog.html); runtime/compiler receipts are emitted. Official evaluator bytes are unchanged and hash checked.

New code/adaptations use Apache-2.0 subject to upstream notices. Code licensing does not grant a blanket relicense of inherited numerical coordinate records. No global theorem, solver invention, packing-optimality or equal-FLOP claim is made.

## Kaggle Submission Recipe

![Recipe](https://storage.googleapis.com/kagglesdsdata/datasets/13027598/21882587/recipe.gif?X-Goog-Algorithm=GOOG4-RSA-SHA256&X-Goog-Credential=databundle-worker-v2%40kaggle-161607.iam.gserviceaccount.com%2F20261109%2Fauto%2Fstorage%2Fgoog4_request&X-Goog-Date=20261109T024915Z&X-Goog-Expires=345600&X-Goog-SignedHeaders=host&X-Goog-)

**Ingredients:**
- A generous scoop of ChatGPT 🧠
- A few tablespoons of Codex 🤖
- A mysterious blend of algorithms and questionable ideas
- A pinch of caffeine ☕
- Several CPUs and GPUs, preferably well-seasoned
- An unreasonable amount of electricity ⚡
- A little luck and a lot of patience 🍀

**Cooking Instructions:**

1. Toss everything into a giant optimization pot and stir until the math starts looking suspicious.
2. Preheat all CPU cores and GPUs to a nice, crispy **70°C**. 🌡️
3. Simmer for several hours, occasionally adding more tokens whenever the results look disappointing.
4. Once all cores are boiling, crank the fans to maximum and let the computational soufflé rise. 🌪️
5. Sprinkle in some random seeds, shake vigorously, and pray to the leaderboard gods.
6. When the smoke clears, carefully extract `submission.csv` and serve immediately. 🏆

**Chef's Note:** Exact measurements are unknown, cooking times vary, and the kitchen is still on fire. 🔥😂

Sharing my latest files with the community. Feel free to improve the recipe, substitute ingredients, or discover an entirely better way to cook these squares!

**Bon appétit, Kagglers!** 🧑‍🍳🚀

# Squares in Squares - Living Atlas of Tight Packings

Start from the attached **Fresh Records, Certified** notebook output, then merge the newest public packings puzzle by puzzle and replay this notebook's own certified improvements.

**Version 118 (10 November):** the attached public outputs complement each other, and the best single one (jazivxt's boxed in sub, 22.2048029) is not the best packing for every `n`.
The merge also considers 0 stored packings (`n` = ) carried forward from earlier versions: local CUDA L-BFGS search, CPU contact-LP polishing, and external packings credited below. Each is retained only where it is the smallest certified packing. The combined result is **22.2048024568**, compared with 22.2048029492 for the best single attached notebook.

Each public packing is admitted only after the same float64 round trip and official certification; border expansion and deletion then run on the merged packings.
Coordinates are round-trip doubles, and centre dilation opens contacts by about `1e-11`. The final CSV is read with pandas' default float64 parser and scored exactly as on Kaggle.
Earlier versions replayed 60 GPU-search gains from 22 October; public packings have since beaten all of them, so their data was replaced by the version 7 improvements.

The default run replays compressed, locally found coordinates. The full search implementation is included below; `RECOMPUTE_SEARCH=True` reruns a bounded search and can take substantially longer.

## Official metric and certification library

Both are embedded verbatim from the certified base. All admission checks use the unchanged competition metric.

## Load the attached base

The parent notebook is the only packing input. Its own credits and source provenance remain applicable.

## Reproducible search code

The extracted CUDA L-BFGS, SAT continuation and contact LP are adapted from lightningv08 (Apache-2.0). Seed selection, checkpointing and the local search schedule are provided here. Floating search candidates still require certification.

## Replay, certify, and write

Every candidate is checked on the exact decimal strings that will be written. The complete 1000-puzzle output is certified again.

## Merge with the newest public packings

Public notebooks move fast. Each attached public output is compared puzzle by puzzle with the packing above.
A smaller public packing replaces ours only if it passes the official metric after the same float64 round trip the scorer uses.
If the best one fails, the next best is tried.

## Score the final float64 file

Default `pd.read_csv` followed by the official `score()` reproduces the leaderboard read path.

## sis-submit — saved v17

https://www.kaggle.com/code/samanyu1808/sis-submit
Source SHA256: a8e0aef8f0983ae9e0c3eb64f31f73eb26694aa01a3b3911a1defcf32ef85c48
Output SHA256: 541bf49cf50a1c4d736a46b55fff452efebc0e89bd411155acde4b2e66c84009

# Squares in Squares: certified packings via stretch + quench

**What this notebook does.** It takes our best per-puzzle packings (dataset `samanyu1808/sis-final-packings`), independently re-verifies every puzzle (bounds, overlap, clearance), recomputes the competition score, explains where the score comes from, and writes `submission.csv`.

**Score** = sum over n=1..1000 of `L/sqrt(n) - 1`, where L is the side of the smallest axis-aligned square containing the n unit squares. Lower is better. Perfect squares n=K^2 contribute 0.

## How the packings were produced
1. **Per-puzzle merge** of ~100 public notebooks and ~25 public datasets, keeping the smallest *certified* side for each n (never the raw smallest: the official metric needs about 1e-11 clearance, so each puzzle is certified in a fresh process).
2. **Stretch + quench.** A packing with tilted arms along two walls is cut by one vertical and one horizontal line. One arm column and one row are copied in, everything past the cut moves by the measured arm pitch, and Evan Daniel's `fq` quench relaxes the overlaps. Kick-and-quench chains (random jitter, random loosen, keep if smaller) refine near-misses.
3. **Clearance enforcement.** Every non-grid puzzle is dilated slightly about the box centre so every pair keeps at least 2e-11 separating-axis clearance.

Credits: public packings from many Kaggle authors; `fq` is Evan Daniel's square-packing (MIT); the stretch idea follows az05192000gmailcom's notebook *22.2427 | Stretching good packings to nearby n*.

## 1. Independent verification
For every puzzle we rebuild the four corners of each rotated unit square, then check (a) the bounding side L, (b) all pairs of nearby squares with the separating-axis test and report the smallest clearance, and (c) that every n has exactly n squares with ids 0..n-1.

## 2. Where the score comes from
Excess `L/sqrt(n) - 1` per puzzle, split into quality tiers. Weak and bad puzzles (more than 1.2% over the area bound) carry almost all of the score, and the leaders' remaining advantage lives there too.

## 3. A few packings
Grey squares are axis-aligned, coloured squares are tilted (colour = tilt angle), red is empty space. The large-n layouts use two tilted arms of different thickness along two walls, ending against an upright block in the corner.

## 4. Write the submission
The certified file is copied byte for byte (no re-formatting of floats, which could change the last digit), and the table of per-puzzle sides is saved next to it.

## 4b. Structure of the packings
Every puzzle is classified from its angles: `grid` (all squares upright), `diag45` (tilted squares at 45 degrees) or `tilted-arms` (arms at other tilts, the stretch-and-quench family). The table shows how many puzzles and how much of the score each family carries.

## 4c. Position against the per-puzzle leaderboard
For every puzzle with a leader row we compare our side with the leader's. `AHEAD` means our L is strictly smaller than the leader's (a per-puzzle record), `tied` means equal within 1e-9. Leader values are a dated snapshot (see METHODS.md). The gap is also expressed in score units, `(L - L_leader)/sqrt(n)`.

## 4d. Lift chains in the leaders' sides
The leaders' sides satisfy `L(n) = L(n') + m` for whole `m` on many pairs (m extra rows and columns of upright squares added around a smaller packing). Our deficit is identical along each chain, so improving one root puzzle should improve every puzzle in its chain. We checked that no puzzle of ours can currently be improved by lifting a smaller packing of ours.

## What did not work (full list in METHODS.md in the dataset)
Own annealing/GPU search beyond n~70, gadget DP rebuilds, contact-LP unjam, boundary LNS, delete-one-and-squeeze, plain random restarts below the grid ceiling for n=12..57. All matched public values or found nothing. The only real gains came from per-puzzle merging of public work and from stretch + quench.

## Remaining gap
The leaders' per-puzzle sides (29 Oct bank) are ~0.03 to 0.04 smaller than ours on about 410 puzzles with n = K^2 + D, K = 20..31, worth about 0.17 of score. Closing that needs a better construction for the tapered arm ends.

Dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/samanyu1808/sis-final-packings; reported license: CC0-1.0. Original component notices remain separately preserved.

Original dataset description:

# Squares in Squares: certified packings

One file, `submission.csv`, in the competition format `id,n,square_id,x,y,angle` (500,500 rows; `angle` in radians, `x,y` are square centres).

## What it is
The best packing found for every n = 1..1000 unit squares, scored by the competition metric as the sum over n of `L/sqrt(n) - 1` (lower is better). Each puzzle was merged per-puzzle from public notebooks and datasets and from our own stretch + quench search, and kept only if it was certified in a fresh process with the current official metric.

## How it was built
1. Per-puzzle merge of ~100 public notebooks and ~25 public datasets, keeping the smallest *certified* side for each n.
2. Stretch + quench: cut a packing with tilted arms along the walls, copy one arm column and one row, shift the rest by the measured arm pitch, then relax with Evan Daniel's `fq` quench (MIT, github.com/evand/square-packing). Kick-and-quench chains refine near-misses.
3. Clearance: every non-grid puzzle is dilated slightly about the box centre so each pair of squares keeps at least 2e-11 SAT clearance, since the Kaggle grader rejects touching squares.
4. Isolated certification: every puzzle is re-checked on its own in a fresh process (0 of 1000 rejected).

## Score history of this dataset
22.2498820 -> 22.2382112 -> 22.2370401 -> 22.2362359 -> 22.2318355 -> 22.2246649 (Boxed In merge, Kaggle-verified) -> 22.2241275 (own chain wins n=417, 595; Kaggle 22.2241274836) -> **22.2234505** (this version, certified locally in isolated per-puzzle runs, 0/1000 rejected).
This version adds: kmmmvs per-puzzle merge (6 puzzles), 18 AWS stretch+quench chain wins at n=650..990, n=109 (strictly below the per-puzzle leaderboard side), n=339 (found by a user's file).

## Files
- `submission.csv`: the packings (500,500 rows).
- `per_puzzle_table.csv`: per n: side, excess, structure family, per-puzzle leaderboard comparison (status AHEAD / tied / behind).
- `lift_chains.csv`: leaderboard sides that equal a smaller puzzle's side plus whole rows (our deficit is identical along a chain).
- `score_history.csv`: certified score after each stage.
- `METHODS.md`: methods, provenance, negative results, caveats.

## Credits
Public packings from many Kaggle authors (Malyshev Danil, Kirill Tymchishin, alex chilton, prvsiyan, az05192000, jazivxt and others), Francisco Couzo's certificates, Evan Daniel's `fq`. Method of stretching by arm columns: az05192000gmailcom, "22.2427 | Stretching good packings to nearby n".

## Caveat
The packings are touching-tight by construction. Use the official metric to verify before reuse.


Original dataset methods:

# Methods, results and negative results

Score = sum over n of L/sqrt(n) - 1 (lower is better). Files: submission.csv (500,500 rows), per_puzzle_table.csv, lift_chains.csv, score_history.csv.

## Pipeline (what actually produced the gains)
1. Per-puzzle merge of ~100 public notebooks/datasets, keeping the smallest side that passes the CURRENT official metric in a fresh process. Biggest steps: jazivxt Boxed In (0.0072), penguin069 portfolio (0.0036), kmmmvs merge (0.00026).
2. Stretch + quench: cut a packing with tilted arms along two walls, copy one arm column and row, shift by the arm pitch, relax with Evan Daniel's fq quench; kick-and-quench chains refine near misses. Own wins: 1e-5..3e-4 each (e.g. n=417, 595, 650, 655, 699, 701, 756...).
3. Compute: local 10 cores, AWS SageMaker (ml.c5.4xlarge CPU, ml.g4dn.xlarge GPU), 5 h cap per job.
4. Clearance: tilted puzzles dilated about the box centre to >= 2e-11 SAT clearance; isolated certification of every puzzle (0/1000 rejected).

## Reverse engineering the per-puzzle leaderboard
Leader sides form lift chains L(n) = L(n') + m (m whole rows added), e.g. 259 -> 445 -> 488 -> 681 -> 734 -> 967 share the same deficit, so one root puzzle controls a whole chain (lift_chains.csv). Only ~23 of ~400 puzzles where we trail fit such a chain; the rest are independent layouts. Per-puzzle leaderboard: we strictly beat the leader at n=109.

## Negative results (do not repeat)
Plain annealing/GPU annealing beyond n~70, hop search, gadget DP rebuilds (matched public), contact-LP unjam, boundary LNS, delete-one-and-squeeze, neighbour transfer, SLP polish, rigid corner-to-corner 45-degree band seeds (relax to ~K+0.95, far worse), jitter/kick-quench on near-ties and on root puzzles of the leaders' lift chains (gain 0), GPU seam DP (2 puzzles, 6e-6), lifting our own packings by whole rows (no gain exists), external catalogs (Ellsworth, jlevy, Couzo, Minuii, tiagocabo and others: no better values).

## Caveats
Packings are touching-tight by construction; verify with the official metric before reuse. Leader values in per_puzzle_table.csv are a snapshot (n<400 taken 7 Nov 2026, others from earlier snapshot) and change daily.

## Provenance (how the data was collected and organised)
- Sources: ~100 public Kaggle notebooks and ~25 datasets (outputs re-downloaded and re-certified; authors credited in the dataset description), Francisco Couzo and Evan Daniel certificates, and our own runs (local 10-core CPU, AWS SageMaker CPU/GPU jobs, chains of stretch + fq quench + kicks).
- Organisation: per-puzzle best-of merge; a packing is accepted only if it passes the current official metric in an isolated process (0/1000 rejected), then dilated to >= 2e-11 SAT clearance and re-certified.
- Collected: 2026-10-24 to 2026-11-07. Leaderboard values: per-puzzle leaderboard notebook by inversion, scraped 2026-11-07 (n<400) and an earlier snapshot for the rest.
- Reproduce: the notebook sis-submit re-verifies bounds, overlap and clearance of every puzzle and recomputes the score.

## 5. Where I stand

## 6. How Different Are My Packings?

Squares all look alike after a while, so I squash each packing into a **tilt map**: an 8 × 8 grid of how far the squares turn, and which way. Then I compare mine with every public packing of the same n.

- **New layout**: no public packing has this arrangement.
- **Flipped arms**: same arms as a public packing, but some turn the other way.
- **Polish**: same layout as a public packing, only tighter.

### 6.1 Tilt changes, all 113 packings

Sorted by score gained. Red: my squares turn more than in the public packing. Blue: less.

- **Polish**: small, local touches.
- **New layout** and **flipped arms**: whole blocks light up.
- **seed**: I polished a looser public packing until it beat the best one. 80 of the 92 polish packings started that way.

### 6.2 Flipped arms

Like a key that only turns after you flip it. Public on the left, mine on the right. **Black outlines** mark the squares that turn the other way.

## 7. How I found them

### 7.1 The pipeline

1. **Merge every public packing.**
   - Every public notebook and dataset, plus the polypack.fly.dev records for n ≤ 500.
   - The shortest one per n becomes my record. Most of my score comes from here.
   - Looser ones with a new layout stay in a pool as seeds. A layout that starts behind can sit in a different valley, a way out of the dip the record is stuck in.
2. **Fault-line DP.** An upright block, the same block shifted along a staircase fault, and small gadgets on the fault. Gadgets are cropped from good packings, so each new public packing brings fresh Lego pieces. *Chris Deotte's idea ([Multi-Gadget Fault DP](https://www.kaggle.com/code/cdeotte/squares-in-squares-multi-gadget-fault-dp-22-48)), written from [alex chilton's starter kit](https://www.kaggle.com/code/alexchilton/squares-101-the-starter-kit-9-500-downloads).*
3. **Stretch.** Take a good packing of a nearby n, cut one tilted arm column in or out, then quench. *From az05192000gmailcom's notebook [Stretching good packings to nearby n](https://www.kaggle.com/code/az05192000gmailcom/22-2401-stretching-good-packings-to-nearby-n).*
4. **fq quench.** Evan Daniel's smooth squeeze, then an exact repair. *From his MIT-licensed [square-packing](https://github.com/evand/square-packing) repository.*
5. **Fixed-angle LP.** Angles fixed, [HiGHS](https://highs.dev) slides the centres into the smallest box. Tiny gains, almost free.

### 7.2 How long each step takes

Orange is search, grey is download and bookkeeping.

### 7.3 Does it scale with n?

Partly. The LP grows with n but stays under a second. Stretch and fq hit a deadline, so they go flat.

### 7.4 Which steps gained the most

- New layouts: Fault-line DP (3 packings)
- Flipped arms: Stretch (6 packings), Fault-line DP (6 packings)

Across all my packings, Fault-line DP carries n 550-700, fq quench leads around n 750-800, and Stretch takes over from n 850.

## 8. What I learned

1. **The gap to the top is about layout.** Polishing a wrong layout is like ironing a shirt that is the wrong size.
2. **Fresh public packings are the best CPU-hour.** One quench of a new one beats hours of hopping on my own.
3. **Re-run fault-line DP after every merge.** New donors, new gadgets.
4. **From-scratch layouts don't work.** They settle one full square too big. New layouts come from cutting, stretching and mixing packings that are already good.
5. **The best packings are one rigid block.** Mine above n 577 are two looser arms. Looseness follows the gap on average, but doesn't decide any single n.

## 9. My dashboard

My mission control. Yes, I check it more often than I should.

## 10. Where I Started: polypack.fly.dev

Before Kaggle there was a website. **sinkomr** pointed me to this competition, and wrote [polypack.fly.dev](https://polypack.fly.dev/), an open record site for packing problems: polygons, circles and balls, squares in squares among them.

Its **Pack@Home** is volunteer computing, SETI@home style. One Node script on your spare cores, and it submits under your name when it beats the site's best.

# A Square Deal

**Official metric on the final file: 22.20029256077** · one best packing per n, then a contact polish · lower is better.

Our polish was worth 1.3e-06 across all 1,000 sizes and on 10 November the public top was 0.0176 ahead of this file, and the merge described in the 10 November section closed it. This notebook measures where polish stops and what a structural move has to do instead.

- On 10 November at 16:20 UTC the public top moved to 22.2003525397 (jonathan1506, stretch + fault-line DP + FQ quench). Our second merge that day took 109 sizes from that output, polished them, and this file is 22.20029256077, 0.0000600 below it. The second-pass section says who gave what.
- Earlier on 10 November the public top was 22.20434. We merged the top 50 public outputs, with our one-size outputs, and polished the 180 sizes that changed; that file was 0.00010 below that top. The 10 November section says who gave what.
- On 7 November we merged the outputs of the top 50 public notebooks size by size with our own search results: 80 sizes came from four public notebooks and 21 from our searches. Taking the best public packing of every size from those 50 notebooks gave 22.22308; this file is 0.00117 lower, from sizes where our own searches still lead.
- Sizes the same count short of a perfect square form a ladder. A size that sits above the line through its neighbours is a target. A search over slab moves, chains and crossovers moved 34 sizes by 0.0035 in total.
- On 10 of 20 sizes we tested, no single contact pays when opened alone. `joint_opening` finds sets that pay only together, from 2 to 18 contacts.
- A force map, read from one LP, shows one load pattern that keeps the box from shrinking.
- The same LP tells you in seconds whether polish can start on a size, so you can skip the sizes where it cannot.
- `square_polish.py`, in this notebook's Output, does all of this on your own file in a few lines.
- The best public packing per size is merged, polished and certified by the official metric, with every source credited.

## verified blend + contact polish · 2026-11-07

The final file scores **22.20029256077** on the pinned official metric, with all 1,000 sizes valid. Rows taken from public sources are copied as they were published. Rows taken from our polished file are written as shortest round-trip binary64 decimals, so a float read returns the same numbers. The next section says what changed, and a later cell runs the polish live on one size.


## use it on your own file

Add this notebook as an input, then:

```python
import sys
from pathlib import Path
sys.path.insert(0, str(next(Path("/kaggle/input").rglob("square_polish.py")).parent))
from square_polish import as_state, contact_prices, joint_opening, polish_file, read_sizes, triage

open_sizes = [row["n"] for row in triage("submission.csv", workers=4) if not row["finished"]]
records = polish_file("submission.csv", "polished.csv", sizes=open_sizes[:20], seconds=120)

state = as_state(read_sizes("submission.csv", [65])[65])
prices = contact_prices(state)                  # one LP per contact
together = joint_opening(state)                 # keep this one to a few hundred squares
```

`triage` solves one LP per size and sorts the sizes by how far the side can fall in that one step. It took 30 seconds for 25 evenly spaced sizes on one laptop core. `finished` means that LP found less than 1e-12 of side, so no first-order move worth polishing. A size whose LP fails, for example because its packing overlaps, comes back with `finished` False and an `error` field.

`polish_file` polishes the sizes you give it and skips the finished ones. It keeps a result only if the official metric accepts it on the exact and the float64 route and the score drops on both. Every other row is written back unchanged, and a size that fails is reported in its record without stopping the rest.

For a single packing use `polish(state, seconds=60)`, where `state` is an (n, 3) array of x, y and angle in radians. That route needs only numpy and scipy. `float_gate.py` and `official_metric.py` sit beside the tool in the Output for the file route.
